claim: Rab proteins are the biggest subfamily within the superfamily of small GTPases.
source: Rab proteins, the biggest subfamily within the superfamily of small GTPases, are major regulators of vesicular trafficking in eukaryotic cells (Takai et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takai et al., 2001

claim: Rab proteins are major regulators of vesicular trafficking in eukaryotic cells.
source: Rab proteins, the biggest subfamily within the superfamily of small GTPases, are major regulators of vesicular trafficking in eukaryotic cells (Takai et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takai et al., 2001

claim: Rab proteins cycle between an inactive GDP-bound and an active GTP-bound state.
source: Like all small GTPases, Rab proteins cycle between an inactive GDP-bound and an active GTP-bound state.
evidence: Established knowledge about small GTPases

claim: The cycling of Rab proteins between GDP-bound and GTP-bound states is tightly regulated and mediated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase activating proteins.
source: The cycling is tightly regulated and mediated by two families of enzymes: guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that catalyze the GDP/GTP exchange and GTPase activating proteins that stimulate GTP hydrolysis (Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stenmark, 2009

claim: GEFs catalyze the GDP/GTP exchange in Rab proteins.
source: The cycling is tightly regulated and mediated by two families of enzymes: guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that catalyze the GDP/GTP exchange and GTPase activating proteins that stimulate GTP hydrolysis (Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stenmark, 2009

claim: GTPase activating proteins stimulate GTP hydrolysis in Rab proteins.
source: The cycling is tightly regulated and mediated by two families of enzymes: guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) that catalyze the GDP/GTP exchange and GTPase activating proteins that stimulate GTP hydrolysis (Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stenmark, 2009

claim: Effector proteins interact specifically with GTP-bound Rab proteins.
source: Additionally, a variety of different effector proteins interact specifically with GTP-bound Rab proteins and mediate their versatile physiological roles in membrane trafficking, including budding of vesicles from a donor membrane, directed transport through the cell and finally tethering and fusion with a target membrane (Grosshans et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosshans et al., 2006

claim: Effector proteins mediate the physiological roles of Rab proteins in membrane trafficking, including budding of vesicles from a donor membrane, directed transport through the cell and tethering and fusion with a target membrane.
source: Additionally, a variety of different effector proteins interact specifically with GTP-bound Rab proteins and mediate their versatile physiological roles in membrane trafficking, including budding of vesicles from a donor membrane, directed transport through the cell and finally tethering and fusion with a target membrane (Grosshans et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosshans et al., 2006

claim: Different effector proteins have been reported to link Rab proteins to the cytoskeleton.
source: Especially in long-distance vesicular transport processes (e.g. in neuronal axons and dendrites), directed vesicular transport along cytoskeletal tracks appears to be an obvious mechanism and, consistently, different effector proteins have been reported to link Rab proteins to the cytoskeleton (Kevenaar and Hoogenraad, 2015; Horgan and McCaffrey, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kevenaar and Hoogenraad, 2015 and Horgan and McCaffrey, 2011

claim: The Mical family is a family of effector proteins that was reported to link Rab proteins and the cytoskeleton.
source: One such family of effector proteins that was reported to link Rab proteins and the cytoskeleton is the Mical (molecules interacting with CasL) family (Figure 1) (Fischer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2005

claim: Most Mical proteins contain an N-terminal monooxygenase domain that was reported to regulate actin dynamics via reversible oxidation of a methionine residue.
source: Most of these Mical proteins contain an N-terminal monooxygenase domain that was reported to regulate actin dynamics via reversible oxidation of a methionine residue (Hung et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013; Hung et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hung et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2013; Hung et al., 2013

claim: All Mical proteins except Mical-cL contain a calponin homology (CH) and a Lin11, Isl-1 and Mec-3 (LIM) domain.
source: Additionally, all Mical proteins except the Mical C-terminal like protein (Mical-cL) contain a calponin homology (CH) and a Lin11, Isl-1 and Mec-3 (LIM) domain that have been reported to assist the interaction with actin and other cytoskeletal proteins, respectively (Giridharan and Caplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giridharan and Caplan, 2014

claim: The CH and LIM domains in Mical proteins have been reported to assist the interaction with actin and other cytoskeletal proteins, respectively.
source: Additionally, all Mical proteins except the Mical C-terminal like protein (Mical-cL) contain a calponin homology (CH) and a Lin11, Isl-1 and Mec-3 (LIM) domain that have been reported to assist the interaction with actin and other cytoskeletal proteins, respectively (Giridharan and Caplan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giridharan and Caplan, 2014

claim: All Mical proteins except Mical-2 contain a C-terminal coiled-coil domain that is also termed domain of unknown function (DUF) 3585.
source: Finally, all except Mical-2 contain a C-terminal coiled-coil domain that is also termed domain of unknown function (DUF) 3585 and that is known to interact with different Rab proteins (Giridharan and Caplan, 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giridharan and Caplan, 2014

claim: The C-terminal coiled-coil domain (DUF3585) in Mical proteins is known to interact with different Rab proteins.
source: Finally, all except Mical-2 contain a C-terminal coiled-coil domain that is also termed domain of unknown function (DUF) 3585 and that is known to interact with different Rab proteins (Giridharan and Caplan, 2014) (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giridharan and Caplan, 2014

claim: According to the SMART database, the DUF3585 domain is present in more than 450 eukaryotic proteins.
source: According to the SMART database (Schultz et al., 1998), this largely uncharacterized DUF3585 domain is present in more than 450 eukaryotic proteins (including 8 human proteins, see Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schultz et al., 1998 and reference to SMART database

claim: The DUF3585 domain is present in 8 human proteins.
source: According to the SMART database (Schultz et al., 1998), this largely uncharacterized DUF3585 domain is present in more than 450 eukaryotic proteins (including 8 human proteins, see Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to SMART database and reference to Figure 1

claim: In humans, the DUF3585 domain is present in the Mical family, the EHBP family, and one uncharacterized protein (C16orf45).
source: In humans, besides the Mical proteins this includes the family of EH (Eps15-homology) domain binding proteins (EHBPs) and one uncharacterized protein (C16orf45; see Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text with reference to Figure 1

claim: EHBPs contain a CH-domain.
source: Interestingly, the EHBPs also contain a CH-domain and have been described to couple vesicular transport to the actin cytoskeleton (Shi et al., 2010; Guilherme et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi et al., 2010 and Guilherme et al., 2004

claim: EHBPs have been described to couple vesicular transport to the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Interestingly, the EHBPs also contain a CH-domain and have been described to couple vesicular transport to the actin cytoskeleton (Shi et al., 2010; Guilherme et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi et al., 2010 and Guilherme et al., 2004

claim: Previously reported interactions of bMERB domain containing proteins with Rab proteins included Rab1, Rab8, Rab10, Rab13, Rab15, Rab35 and Rab36.
source: Previously reported interactions of different bMERB domain containing proteins with Rab proteins included Rab1, Rab8, Rab10, Rab13, Rab15, Rab35 and Rab36 (Giridharan and Caplan, 2014; Shi et al., 2010), although not all possible combinations of the effectors and the different Rab proteins were tested nor interactions quantified.
evidence: Supported by citations to Giridharan and Caplan, 2014 and Shi et al., 2010

claim: Stable complex formation was detected between bMERB domains and Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 via analytical size exclusion chromatography.
source: In these experiments, stable complex formation was detected with Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 (since Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 are closely related in amino acid sequence, we refer to them as the Rab8 family [Klöpper et al., 2012]).
evidence: Experimental data from analytical size exclusion chromatography experiments described in the manuscript

claim: Rab1 failed to form stable complexes with bMERB-domain proteins, indicating low affinity.
source: Rab1, however, failed to form stable complexes with bMERB-domain proteins, indicating low affinity.
evidence: Experimental observation from analytical size exclusion chromatography

claim: Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 are closely related in amino acid sequence and are referred to as the Rab8 family.
source: In these experiments, stable complex formation was detected with Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 (since Rab8, Rab10, Rab13 and Rab15 are closely related in amino acid sequence, we refer to them as the Rab8 family [Klöpper et al., 2012]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klöpper et al., 2012

claim: KD values of 2.2–5.2 µM were observed for Rab1 binding to the bMERB domains of Mical proteins.
source: Whereas we observed KD values of 2.2–5.2 µM for Rab1 binding to the bMERB domains of Mical proteins and no detectable binding of Rab1 to the bMERB domains of EHBPs (Table 1 and Figure 2a), we detected strong binding and ca. 100 nanomolar affinities for Rab8 and the different bMERB domains (see Table 1 and Figure 2b).
evidence: ITC measurements reported in Table 1 and Figure 2a

claim: No detectable binding of Rab1 to the bMERB domains of EHBPs was observed.
source: Whereas we observed KD values of 2.2–5.2 µM for Rab1 binding to the bMERB domains of Mical proteins and no detectable binding of Rab1 to the bMERB domains of EHBPs (Table 1 and Figure 2a), we detected strong binding and ca. 100 nanomolar affinities for Rab8 and the different bMERB domains (see Table 1 and Figure 2b).
evidence: ITC measurements reported in Table 1 and Figure 2a

claim: Strong binding with ca. 100 nanomolar affinities was detected for Rab8 and the different bMERB domains.
source: Whereas we observed KD values of 2.2–5.2 µM for Rab1 binding to the bMERB domains of Mical proteins and no detectable binding of Rab1 to the bMERB domains of EHBPs (Table 1 and Figure 2a), we detected strong binding and ca. 100 nanomolar affinities for Rab8 and the different bMERB domains (see Table 1 and Figure 2b).
evidence: ITC measurements reported in Table 1 and Figure 2b

claim: All members of the Rab8 family bound Mical-cL with high nanomolar affinities.
source: Using Mical-cL as one representative of the bMERB family, we saw that all members of the Rab8 family bound Mical-cL with high nanomolar affinities, compared to Rab1 (KD = 5.2 µM) and Rab35 (KD = 1.8 µM; Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: ITC measurements reported in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The highest affinity observed was that of Rab15 and Mical-cL with a KD of 33 nM.
source: The highest affinity observed was that of Rab15 and Mical-cL with a KD of 33 nM.
evidence: ITC measurement data

claim: Rab1a, Rab1b and Rab35 were previously shown not to interact with EHBP1/EHBP1L1.
source: In accordance with the strong specificity of EHBPs towards the Rab8 family, Rab1a, Rab1b and Rab35 (a close relative of Rab1 which is also sometimes referred to as Rab1c) were previously shown not to interact with EHBP1/EHBP1L1 (Shi et al., 2010; Nakajo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi et al., 2010 and Nakajo et al., 2016

claim: Rab35 is a close relative of Rab1 which is also sometimes referred to as Rab1c.
source: In accordance with the strong specificity of EHBPs towards the Rab8 family, Rab1a, Rab1b and Rab35 (a close relative of Rab1 which is also sometimes referred to as Rab1c) were previously shown not to interact with EHBP1/EHBP1L1 (Shi et al., 2010; Nakajo et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated in text with supporting citations

claim: A 2:1 stoichiometry binding was observed for Rab8 and Mical-1, Mical-3 and EHBP1L1 in ITC experiments.
source: Whereas Rab8 bound in a 1:1 stoichiometry to Mical-cL and EHBP1, a 2:1 stoichiometry binding was observed for Mical-1, Mical-3 and EHBP1L1 (Table 1 and Figure 2b).
evidence: ITC experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2b

claim: Rab8 bound in a 1:1 stoichiometry to Mical-cL and EHBP1.
source: Whereas Rab8 bound in a 1:1 stoichiometry to Mical-cL and EHBP1, a 2:1 stoichiometry binding was observed for Mical-1, Mical-3 and EHBP1L1 (Table 1 and Figure 2b).
evidence: ITC experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2b

claim: For Rab8 and Mical-1/Mical-3, the ITC experiments show one high-affinity enthalpy-driven and one lower affinity entropy-driven binding site.
source: For Rab8 and Mical-1/Mical-3, the ITC experiments show one high-affinity enthalpy-driven and one lower affinity entropy-driven binding site, compared to two binding sites with similar affinity for Rab8 and EHBP1L1.
evidence: ITC experimental data

claim: For Rab8 and EHBP1L1, two binding sites with similar affinity were observed.
source: For Rab8 and Mical-1/Mical-3, the ITC experiments show one high-affinity enthalpy-driven and one lower affinity entropy-driven binding site, compared to two binding sites with similar affinity for Rab8 and EHBP1L1.
evidence: ITC experimental data

claim: aSEC experiments confirmed a 2:1 stoichiometry for the Rab8:EHBP1L1 and Rab8:Mical-1 complexes.
source: These experiments clearly confirmed the aforementioned differences in the stoichiometry of binding with a 2:1 stoichiometry being observed for the Rab8:EHBP1L1 and Rab8:Mical-1 complexes, but not for others tested.
evidence: aSEC experimental data shown in Figure 2c

claim: The low affinity second binding site of Mical-3 (KD = 4.4 µM) could not be detected in aSEC experiments, suggesting dynamic complex formation with a large koff.
source: The low affinity second binding site of Mical-3 (KD = 4.4 µM as determined by ITC, Table 1) could also not be detected in these experiments, suggesting dynamic complex formation with a large koff.
evidence: Inference from ITC and aSEC experimental data

claim: Mical-1 and EHBP1L1 contain two binding sites that bind Rab8 with high affinity.
source: These data show that Mical-1 and EHBP1L1 contain two binding sites that bind Rab8 with high affinity, whereas Mical-3 (and possibly Mical-cL and EHBP1) contain one high affinity and a second lower affinity binding site for Rab8.
evidence: Conclusion from ITC and aSEC experimental data

claim: Mical-3 (and possibly Mical-cL and EHBP1) contain one high affinity and a second lower affinity binding site for Rab8.
source: These data show that Mical-1 and EHBP1L1 contain two binding sites that bind Rab8 with high affinity, whereas Mical-3 (and possibly Mical-cL and EHBP1) contain one high affinity and a second lower affinity binding site for Rab8.
evidence: Conclusion from ITC and aSEC experimental data with speculation about Mical-cL and EHBP1

claim: Recent studies on Mical-L2 dependent GLUT4 translocation showed that trafficking was dependent on a concerted action of Rab8 and Rab13.
source: In accordance with this idea, recent studies on Mical-L2 dependent GLUT4 translocation showed that trafficking was dependent on a concerted action of Rab8 and Rab13 (Sun et al., 2010, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2010, 2016

claim: aSEC experiments confirmed the formation of a ternary complex of Rab8:Mical-1:Rab13 as well as Rab8:EHBP1L1:Rab13.
source: We consequently also tested whether the effector proteins might be able to simultaneously bind two different Rab proteins in a 1:1:1 (RabX:effector:RabY) complex using both Rab8 and Rab13 and the corresponding aSEC experiments clearly confirmed the formation of a ternary complex of Rab8:Mical-1:Rab13 as well as Rab8:EHBP1L1:Rab13 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: aSEC experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The structure of Mical-31841-1990 containing the whole predicted bMERB domain was solved with a resolution of 2.7 Å.
source: We succeeded in crystallizing a selenomethionine derivative of Mical-31841-1990 containing the whole predicted bMERB domain and solved the structure with a resolution of 2.7 Å (data and refinement statistics are shown in Table 2).
evidence: X-ray crystallography data shown in Table 2

claim: The asymmetric unit of Mical-3 contains two copies that form a central 4-stranded coiled-coil composed of α-helices 2 and 3 of each monomer flanked by α-helices 1 on both sides.
source: The asymmetric unit contains two copies of Mical-3 that form a central 4-stranded coiled-coil composed of α-helices 2 and 3 of each monomer flanked by α-helices 1 on both sides (Figure 4a).
evidence: Structural data from X-ray crystallography shown in Figure 4a

claim: Each monomer of Mical-3 consists of a central helix (α2, residues K1891-R1937) and N- and C-terminal helices folding back on this central helix.
source: Overall, the structure shows that each monomer consists of a central helix (α2, residues K1891-R1937) and N- and C-terminal helices folding back on this central helix.
evidence: Structural data from X-ray crystallography

claim: In all structures (Rab1:Mical-cL, Rab8:Mical-cL and Rab10:Mical-cL), one Rab protein was found bound to one molecule of Mical-cL.
source: In all structures (Rab1:Mical-cL, Rab8:Mical-cL and Rab10:Mical-cL) we found one Rab protein bound to one molecule of Mical-cL (Figure 5a), in agreement with the previous observations that all Rab proteins tested bind only one site in Mical-cL.
evidence: X-ray crystallography structural data shown in Figure 5a

claim: Most interactions were visible between the Rab proteins and α-helix 3 of Mical-cL with some additional contributing residues from α-helix 2.
source: Most interactions were visible between the Rab proteins and α-helix 3 of Mical-cL with some additional contributing residues from α-helix 2, forming extensive contacts involving residues within switch I and II of the Rab proteins (Figure 5b).
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography shown in Figure 5b

claim: Hydrophobic interactions between the hydrophobic patch II in Mical-cL and residues from Rabs forming a hydrophobic pocket and a triad of aromatic amino acids were observed in the Rab:Mical-cL structures.
source: In all cases, hydrophobic interactions between the hydrophobic patch II in Mical-cL and residues from Rabs forming a hydrophobic pocket (residues Ile43, Phe70 and Ile73 in Rab8) and a triad of aromatic amino acids (Phe45, Trp62, Tyr77 in Rab8) known from all Rab:effector complexes solved to date (Itzen and Goody, 2011) were also observed in the Rab:Mical-cL structures.
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography with reference to known Rab:effector complexes

claim: The Rab-binding interface in Mical-cL has a substantial overlap with the dimer interface observed in the structure of Mical-3.
source: Interestingly, the Rab-binding interface in Mical-cL has a substantial overlap with the dimer interface observed in the structure of Mical-3 above.
evidence: Comparison of structural data from X-ray crystallography

claim: Mical-1 runs as an apparent monomer in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein induces a clear shift to higher molecular weight.
source: Additionally, even though all Mical constructs used have a similar molecular weight of ~18 kDa, whereas Mical-1 runs as an apparent monomer in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein induces a clear shift to higher molecular weight, both Mical-3 and Mical-cL run as apparent dimers in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein disrupts the dimer, thus not leading to a shift in retention time upon complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: aSEC experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Both Mical-3 and Mical-cL run as apparent dimers in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein disrupts the dimer.
source: Additionally, even though all Mical constructs used have a similar molecular weight of ~18 kDa, whereas Mical-1 runs as an apparent monomer in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein induces a clear shift to higher molecular weight, both Mical-3 and Mical-cL run as apparent dimers in aSEC and binding of a Rab protein disrupts the dimer, thus not leading to a shift in retention time upon complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: aSEC experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Extensive interaction of Mical-cL with RabSF1 (Tyr6, Asp7, Leu9, Lys11 in Rab10) and (less interactions) with RabSF2 (Asp31, Ser40 in Rab10) was observed in the Rab:Mical-cL structures.
source: In the Rab:Mical-cL structures, we observed extensive interaction of Mical-cL with RabSF1 (Tyr6, Asp7, Leu9, Lys11 in Rab10) and (less interactions) with RabSF2 (Asp31, Ser40 in Rab10).
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography

claim: The sequence alignment of different Rab proteins shows strong conservation of the interacting amino acids within RabSF1 and RabSF2 motifs amongst Rab1 and Rab8 family members that interact with bMERB domains, but not for other Rab proteins.
source: Accordingly, the sequence alignment of different Rab proteins (Figure 5) shows strong conservation of the interacting amino acids within these motifs amongst Rab1 (Rab1a/b, Rab35) and Rab8 (Rab8a/b, Rab10, Rab13, Rab15) family members that interact with bMERB domains, but not for other Rab proteins (a comparative scheme of the residues involved in interactions in the different complexes is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The main chain atoms of the N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif can be traced in the electron density and seem to interact with amino acids within α-helix 1 and 2 of Mical-cL.
source: However, we observed that the main chain atoms of the N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif can be traced in the electron density and seem to interact with amino acids within α-helix 1 and 2 of Mical-cL, even though the electron density in this region did not allow a precise localization of the side chains.
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography electron density maps

claim: Slightly different orientations of the α-helices 1 and 2 were observed, adopting a position slightly further away from Rab1 compared to Rab8 and Rab10.
source: In contrast to the main interacting helix α3, which adopts a similar position in all three structures, we observed slightly different orientations of the α-helices 1 and 2, adopting a position slightly further away from Rab1 compared to Rab8 and Rab10 (Figure 5a).
evidence: Structural comparison from X-ray crystallography shown in Figure 5a

claim: Rab1 contains a glutamate near the N-terminus (Glu4), while all Rab8 family members contain one or two lysine residues in this region.
source: Interestingly, whereas Rab1 contains a glutamate near the N-terminus (Glu4), all Rab8 family members contain one or (in the case of Rab10) two lysine residues in this region that point towards a negatively charged patch in Mical-cL (Figure 5b).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 5b

claim: Rab35 contains an Arg residue within the N-terminal region and displays a slightly higher affinity towards Mical-cL compared to Rab1.
source: Additionally, Rab35 contains an Arg residue within this N-terminal region and also displays a slightly higher affinity towards Mical-cL compared to Rab1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural and ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The x-ray crystallographic structure of Rab1R8N (a chimera of Rab1 containing the 4 N-terminal aa of Rab8) in complex with Mical-cL showed that the helices 1 and 2 move closer and adopt a similar conformation as observed in the structures of Rab8:Mical-cL and Rab10:Mical-cL.
source: The x-ray crystallographic structure of this Rab1 chimera (termed Rab1R8N) in complex with Mical-cL clearly showed that the helices 1 and 2 move closer and adopt a similar conformation as observed in the structures of Rab8:Mical-cL and Rab10:Mical-cL (Figure 5a).
evidence: X-ray crystallography structural data shown in Figure 5a

claim: ITC measurements showed that the Rab1R8N chimera had an approximately five-fold increased binding affinity compared to Rab1.
source: Additionally, ITC measurements showed that the chimera had an approximately five-fold increased binding affinity compared to Rab1 (Figure 5c).
evidence: ITC experimental data shown in Figure 5c

claim: The chimera Rab1R8N bound both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 in aSEC experiments, whereas Rab1 did not.
source: In contrast to Rab1, the chimera Rab1R8N bound both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 in aSEC experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), thus clearly indicating that the N-terminus is important for the interaction and contributes to the observed specificity of bMERB domains towards Rab proteins.
evidence: aSEC experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b

claim: The N-terminus is important for the interaction and contributes to the observed specificity of bMERB domains towards Rab proteins.
source: In contrast to Rab1, the chimera Rab1R8N bound both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 in aSEC experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), thus clearly indicating that the N-terminus is important for the interaction and contributes to the observed specificity of bMERB domains towards Rab proteins.
evidence: Conclusion from aSEC and structural data

claim: The structure of Mical-1 in complex with Rab10 showed two molecules of Rab10 bound to Mical-1.
source: Crystallization conditions were found using a complex of Rab101–175 and the RBD of Mical-1 (residues 918–1067), yielding crystals that diffracted to a resolution of 2.8 Angstrom at a synchrotron X-ray source and the resulting structure indeed showed two molecules of Rab10 bound to Mical-1 (Figure 6a).
evidence: X-ray crystallography structural data shown in Figure 6a

claim: One Rab binding site in Mical-1 is composed of the N-terminal half of the bMERB domain (α-helix 1 and the first half of α-helix 2), while the other comprises the C-terminal half (second half of α-helix 2 and α-helix 3).
source: In addition to the binding site corresponding to the one previously observed in Mical-cL, an additional binding site was identified: Whereas this site is composed of the N-terminal half of the bMERB domain (α-helix 1 and the first half of α-helix 2), the Rab binding site observed in both Mical-1 and Mical-cL comprises the C-terminal half (second half of α-helix 2 and α-helix 3).
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography

claim: Upon superimposition of both binding sites in Mical-1, the strong similarity becomes obvious and the helices from both binding sites adopt very similar positions.
source: Upon superimposition of both binding sites, the strong similarity becomes obvious and the helices from both binding sites adopt very similar positions.
evidence: Structural comparison from X-ray crystallography shown in Figure 6a

claim: The interactions are highly similar in both binding sites of Mical-1.
source: Furthermore, the interactions are highly similar in both cases as can be seen in the close-up view on the right (similar Rab-interacting residues within binding site 1 and 2 are shown in blue and green, respectively).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: Deletion of either α-helix 1 or α-helix 3 impairs binding to binding site 1 or 2, respectively.
source: Consistent with the localization of the two separate binding sites within the N-terminal and the C-terminal half of the bMERB domain, respectively, deletion constructs lacking either α-helix 1 (Mical960–1067) or α-helix 3 (Mical-1918–1020) displayed a clear 1:1 stoichiometry of Rab binding both in aSEC and ITC experiments (Figure 6c).
evidence: aSEC and ITC experimental data shown in Figure 6c

claim: The ITC data allowed allocation of the high affinity binding to the C-terminal binding site and the lower affinity binding to the N-terminal binding site.
source: Furthermore, the ITC data allowed us to clearly allocate the high affinity binding to the C-terminal binding site and the lower affinity binding to the N-terminal binding site.
evidence: ITC experimental data

claim: The strong conservation of interacting residues between both sites as well as the structural conservation of the binding sites suggests that this family of Rab binding proteins must have evolved via gene duplication.
source: In summary, the strong conservation of interacting residues between both sites as well as the structural conservation of the binding sites lead us to conclude that this family of Rab binding proteins must have evolved via gene duplication (Figure 6d).
evidence: Inference from structural and sequence analysis shown in Figure 6d

claim: The strong conservation of interacting residues between the two separate binding sites in Mical-1 and between the different bMERB domains suggests that all of these proteins contain a second (possibly low affinity) binding site.
source: Furthermore the strong conservation of interacting residues not only between the two separate binding sites in Mical-1, but also between the different bMERB domains (see alignments in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3) suggests that all of these proteins contain a second (possibly low affinity) binding site.
evidence: Inference from sequence alignments shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 3

claim: The bMERB domains probably constitute a Rab8-effector family involved in endosomal trafficking.
source: The results show that the domains probably constitute a Rab8-effector family involved in endosomal trafficking, and the Rab-binding specificity can be well explained from the 3-dimensional structures of complexes determined in this work.
evidence: Conclusion from structural and biochemical data

claim: The Rab-binding specificity of bMERB domains can be well explained from the 3-dimensional structures of complexes determined in this work.
source: The results show that the domains probably constitute a Rab8-effector family involved in endosomal trafficking, and the Rab-binding specificity can be well explained from the 3-dimensional structures of complexes determined in this work.
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography

claim: At least some bMERB domains contain two separate binding sites for Rab-proteins.
source: Furthermore, we show that at least some of these domains contain two separate binding sites for Rab-proteins, suggesting previously unknown functions, as discussed below.
evidence: Structural and biochemical data

claim: The strong similarity between the 2 binding sites within one effector domain strongly suggests an evolutionary development via gene duplication.
source: The strong similarity between the 2 binding sites within one effector domain strongly suggests an evolutionary development via gene duplication.
evidence: Inference from structural and sequence analysis

claim: The high specificity of the effector domains towards Rab8 family members can be well explained from the structural analysis of Rab:bMERB complexes.
source: The high specificity of the effector domains towards Rab8 family members can be well explained from the structural analysis of Rab:bMERB complexes.
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography

claim: Specificity-determining interactions were seen between the effector domains and the RabSF1 and RabSF2 motifs.
source: Specificity-determining interactions were seen between the effector domains and the RabSF1 and RabSF2 motifs.
evidence: Structural analysis from X-ray crystallography

claim: The N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif contribute to the specificity of bMERB domains, allowing them to distinguish Rab1- and Rab8-family members.
source: In this regard, we showed that the N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif contribute to this specificity, an observation that has previously not been made in other Rab:effector interactions.
evidence: Structural and biochemical data from this study

claim: The observation that N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif contribute to specificity has previously not been made in other Rab:effector interactions.
source: In this regard, we showed that the N-terminal residues preceding the RabSF1 motif contribute to this specificity, an observation that has previously not been made in other Rab:effector interactions.
evidence: Comparison with existing literature on Rab:effector interactions

claim: The 3-dimensional structures of the effector domains solved in this work showed a solely α-helical fold common to many other Rab effector proteins.
source: The 3-dimensional structures of the effector domains solved in this work showed a solely α-helical fold common to many other Rab effector proteins (Oesterlin et al., 2014).
evidence: Structural data from this study with reference to Oesterlin et al., 2014

claim: The main interacting helix in Rab:bMERB complexes adopts a similar position to that of the main interacting helix in the structures of Rab27:Slp2-a, Rab27:Slac2a/melanophilin and Rab3:Rabphilin-3a.
source: Further comparison with other known Rab:effector structures showed that the main interacting helix in Rab:bMERB complexes (e.g. α-helix 3 in Mical-cL) adopts a similar position to that of the main interacting helix in the structures of Rab27:Slp2-a (Chavas et al., 2008), Rab27:Slac2a/melanophilin (Kukimoto-Niino et al., 2008) and Rab3:Rabphilin-3a (Ostermeier and Brunger, 1999) (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for a comparison).
evidence: Structural comparison with cited structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: In Rab27:Slp2-a, Rab27:Slac2a and Rab:bMERB structures, the Arg/Lys contacting Asp45 in Rabs is conserved in the effector proteins.
source: Interestingly, in all three examples, the Arg/Lys contacting Asp45 in our Mical:Rab structures is also conserved in these effector proteins, and the Asp/Asn following this basic residue and contacting Gln61 in Rabs is conserved in both Slp2-a and Slac2a.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis

claim: These effector domains (Slp2-a, Slac2a) display similar binding affinities as bMERB domains towards their cognate Rabs (KD = 13.4 nM for Rab27:Slp2-a, KD = 112 nM for Rab27:Slac2-a/melanophilin).
source: Intriguingly, these effector domains also display similar binding affinities as bMERB domains towards their cognate Rabs (KD = 13.4 nM for Rab27:Slp2-a, KD = 112 nM for Rab27:Slac2-a/melanophilin) (Fukuda, 2006), and these are amongst the highest affinities observed for Rab:effector interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fukuda, 2006

claim: The affinities of Rab27:Slp2-a and Rab27:Slac2-a/melanophilin are amongst the highest affinities observed for Rab:effector interactions.
source: Intriguingly, these effector domains also display similar binding affinities as bMERB domains towards their cognate Rabs (KD = 13.4 nM for Rab27:Slp2-a, KD = 112 nM for Rab27:Slac2-a/melanophilin) (Fukuda, 2006), and these are amongst the highest affinities observed for Rab:effector interactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fukuda, 2006 and general knowledge

claim: Rab:effector complexes that were previously characterized display either a 1:1 or 2:2 stoichiometry.
source: In contrast to the bMERB domain proteins, Rab:effector complexes that were previously characterized display either a 1:1 or 2:2 stoichiometry, where the 2:2 complexes are usually formed by a central effector dimer with symmetrical binding interfaces on both sites (Oesterlin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oesterlin et al., 2014

claim: Multivalent Rab effector proteins have been described previously, including Rab4 and Rab5 binding to Rabaptin-5, Rab6 and Rab11 binding to Rab6IP1, and Gcc185 with five sites binding to multiple Rabs.
source: On the other hand, multivalent Rab effector proteins have been described previously (examples are Rab4 and Rab5 binding to Rabaptin-5 (Vitale et al., 1998), Rab6 and Rab11 binding to Rab6IP1 (Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007) or the extreme case of Gcc185 with five sites binding to Rab1a/b, Rab2a/b, Rab6a/b, Rab9a/b, Rab15, Rab27, Rab30, Rab33, Rab35 and Rab36 (Hayes et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vitale et al., 1998; Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007; Hayes et al., 2009

claim: All previously described multivalent Rab effectors contain separate Rab-binding domains, each in turn only binding one Rab protein.
source: However, all of these effectors contain separate Rab-binding domains, each in turn only binding one Rab protein.
evidence: Comparison with existing literature on multivalent Rab effectors

claim: This work constitutes the first description of two Rab proteins binding a single effector domain.
source: The work presented constitutes the first description of two Rab proteins binding a single effector domain.
evidence: Conclusion from this study's findings

claim: Bivalent effectors could link Rab-decorated vesicles to a target membrane or other vesicles via a central bivalent effector.
source: Such functions could include linking Rab-decorated vesicles to a target membrane or other vesicles via a central bivalent effector.
evidence: Speculation about possible functions

claim: Concerted Rab cascades and feedback loops have been observed with effector domains fused to GEFs or GAPs of one Rab acting upstream or downstream of a second Rab.
source: On the other hand, concerted Rab cascades and feedback loops have been observed with effector domains fused to GEFs or GAPs of one Rab acting upstream or downstream of a second Rab, helping to recruit or remove Rab proteins from a certain membrane (Pfeffer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pfeffer, 2013

claim: Bivalent effectors could act in a positive feedback loop, initially being recruited by activated Rab proteins and subsequently helping in the recruitment and stabilization of further Rabs at this site to establish Rab membrane microdomains.
source: Bivalent effectors could act in a similar manner in a positive feedback loop, initially being recruited by activated Rab proteins and subsequently helping in the recruitment and stabilization of further Rabs at this site to establish Rab membrane microdomains (Pfeffer, 2013).
evidence: Speculation with reference to Pfeffer, 2013

claim: The presence of one high affinity and one low affinity Rab binding site could enhance the formation of Rab microdomains.
source: In fact, the presence of one high affinity and one low affinity Rab binding site as observed in some bMERB effectors could further enhance the formation of Rab microdomains: Whereas the Rab bound to the high affinity site would essentially stay bound within physiologically relevant timescales, the additional Rab protein recruited by the low affinity site could dissociate again and recruit another effector molecule via the high affinity site, thus helping to concentrate Rabs within small areas on the membrane.
evidence: Speculation based on observed binding affinities

claim: bMERB domain containing effectors might fulfill functions in vesicular trafficking and act as effector Rab hubs, similar to the suggested function of Rab6IP linking Rab6 and Rab11 mediated vesicular trafficking events.
source: Additionally and similar to the suggested function of Rab6IP linking Rab6 and Rab11 mediated vesicular trafficking events (Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007), bMERB domain containing effectors might fulfill analogous functions in vesicular trafficking and act as effector Rab hubs.
evidence: Speculation with reference to Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2007

claim: The possible importance of concerted membrane recruitment cascades of Rabs and other proteins involved in membrane trafficking has been previously highlighted for Mical-L1 connecting Rab35 and Rab8.
source: The possible importance of such concerted membrane recruitment cascades of Rabs and other proteins involved in membrane trafficking has been previously highlighted for Mical-L1 connecting Rab35 and Rab8, and this was aptly referred to as a membrane hub (Rahajeng et al., 2012; Giridharan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rahajeng et al., 2012 and Giridharan et al., 2012

claim: It was shown that Mical-L1 is recruited to recycling endosomes by Rab35 and subsequently recruits other Rab proteins (Rab8, Rab13 and Rab36).
source: In another study it was shown that Mical-L1 is recruited to recycling endosomes by Rab35 and subsequently recruits other Rab proteins (Rab8, Rab13 and Rab36) (Kobayashi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kobayashi et al., 2014

claim: The 2 separate binding sites presumably present in Mical-L1 and Mical-L2 could help in establishing a concerted action of two Rabs by connecting them via one bivalent effector protein in an (intermediate) 1:1:1 complex.
source: However, our data now show how the 2 separate binding sites presumably also present in Mical-L1 and Mical-L2 (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1) could help in establishing this concerted action of two Rabs by connecting them via one bivalent effector protein in an (intermediate) 1:1:1 complex, thus explaining for the first time the structural and biochemical basis of the Rab hub function.
evidence: Inference from structural and biochemical data with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The strong sequence homology of different bMERB domains including both binding sites and the fact that all Rab8 family proteins reported to interact with Micals/EHBPs are implicated in different steps of endocytic trafficking points towards an important function of Micals/EHBPs in sorting of endocytic cargo with different destinations in the cell.
source: The strong sequence homology of different bMERB domains including both binding sites and the fact that all Rab8 family proteins reported to interact with Micals/EHBPs are implicated in different steps of endocytic trafficking (Wandinger-Ness and Zerial, 2014) as well as previously published data thus points towards an important function of Micals/EHBPs in sorting of endocytic cargo with different destinations in the cell.
evidence: Inference from sequence analysis and literature with citation to Wandinger-Ness and Zerial, 2014

claim: Previous studies have shown that the bMERB domains in Micals can bind to their CH/LIM domains, forming an auto-inhibited intramolecular interaction that can be released by competitive binding of Rab proteins.
source: Previous studies have shown that the bMERB domains in Micals can bind to their CH/LIM domains, forming an auto-inhibited intramolecular interaction that can be released by competitive binding of Rab proteins, thus allowing for the interaction with actin only after binding of Rabs (Sun et al., 2016; Sakane et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2016; Sakane et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2008

claim: The two binding sites in bMERB domains might have separate functions, serving as a membrane recruitment site by Rabs via one site and release of the auto-inhibition due to competitive binding of the CH/LIM domains and Rabs at the second binding site.
source: The two binding sites might therefore also have separate functions, serving as a membrane recruitment site by Rabs via one site (presumably the high-affinity binding site) and release of the auto-inhibition due to competitive binding of the CH/LIM domains and Rabs at the second binding site.
evidence: Speculation about possible functional implications

claim: The two binding sites in bMERB domains share a strong similarity and bind Rab proteins via similar residues within the interaction surfaces.
source: In the last part of the study, we have shown that the two binding sites share a strong similarity and bind Rab proteins via similar residues within the interaction surfaces, thus indicating that the RBD have evolved via duplication of a common ancestor supersecondary structure element (Figure 6d) (Söding and Lupas, 2003).
evidence: Structural analysis with reference to Söding and Lupas, 2003

claim: The RBD have evolved via duplication of a common ancestor supersecondary structure element.
source: In the last part of the study, we have shown that the two binding sites share a strong similarity and bind Rab proteins via similar residues within the interaction surfaces, thus indicating that the RBD have evolved via duplication of a common ancestor supersecondary structure element (Figure 6d) (Söding and Lupas, 2003).
evidence: Inference from structural analysis with reference to Söding and Lupas, 2003

claim: The underlying single α-hairpin motifs making up the separate Rab-binding sites are known from other Rab-effectors such as Rabenosyn-5.
source: The underlying single α-hairpin motifs making up the separate Rab-binding sites are known from other Rab-effectors such as Rabenosyn-5 (Khan and Ménétrey, 2013; Eathiraj et al., 2005), and the resulting fused α-hairpins observed in Micals and EHBPs strongly resemble the architecture of spectrin repeats, each being connected via one continuous helix (Han et al., 2007; Pascual et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khan and Ménétrey, 2013; Eathiraj et al., 2005; Han et al., 2007; Pascual et al., 1997

claim: The resulting fused α-hairpins observed in Micals and EHBPs strongly resemble the architecture of spectrin repeats, each being connected via one continuous helix.
source: The underlying single α-hairpin motifs making up the separate Rab-binding sites are known from other Rab-effectors such as Rabenosyn-5 (Khan and Ménétrey, 2013; Eathiraj et al., 2005), and the resulting fused α-hairpins observed in Micals and EHBPs strongly resemble the architecture of spectrin repeats, each being connected via one continuous helix (Han et al., 2007; Pascual et al., 1997).
evidence: Structural comparison with citations to Han et al., 2007 and Pascual et al., 1997

claim: The duplication of the bMERB domain must have occurred early in evolution in one common ancestor bMERB domain.
source: Because of the strong similarity between the repeats of the different isoforms of Micals and EHBPs, but less similarity between both repeats within the bMERB domains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), we suggest that the duplication must have occurred early in evolution in one common ancestor bMERB domain.
evidence: Inference from sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b

claim: The two repeats in bMERB domains have diverged in terms of overall sequence, but the ability to bind Rab proteins has remained in at least some cases.
source: The two repeats have since diverged in terms of overall sequence, but the ability to bind Rab proteins has remained in at least some cases, as shown in this study.
evidence: Conclusion from this study's findings

claim: Both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 can be farnesylated and geranylgeranylated by FTase and GGTase I, respectively, in vitro.
source: In vitro, both proteins can be farnesylated and geranylgeranylated by FTase and GGTase I, respectively.
evidence: In vitro prenylation experiments

claim: EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 show preferential farnesylation in accordance with the C-terminal amino acids of the CaaX-boxes being glutamine or serine.
source: However, in accordance with the C-terminal amino acids of the CaaX-boxes being glutamine or serine (Zhang and Casey, 1996), we observed preferential farnesylation (Figure 3a).
evidence: In vitro prenylation experiments shown in Figure 3a with reference to Zhang and Casey, 1996

claim: Experiments clearly showed a CaaX-box dependent localization of both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 to intracellular structures resembling endosomes.
source: These experiments clearly showed a CaaX-box dependent localization of both proteins to intracellular structures resembling endosomes (Figure 3b), as previously reported for the full length proteins (Shi et al., 2010).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3b with reference to Shi et al., 2010

claim: Both EHBP1 and EHBP1L1 showed strong colocalization with constitutively active Rab8 and Rab10 (Rab8Q67L and Rab10Q68L).
source: Additionally, both proteins showed strong colocalization with constitutively active Rab8 and Rab10 (i.e. Rab8Q67L and Rab10Q68L), both known to act at endosomes (Figure 3c), further supporting the function of this family of effector proteins as Rab8-family binding partners.
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3c

claim: Rab8 and Rab10 are known to act at endosomes.
source: Additionally, both proteins showed strong colocalization with constitutively active Rab8 and Rab10 (i.e. Rab8Q67L and Rab10Q68L), both known to act at endosomes (Figure 3c), further supporting the function of this family of effector proteins as Rab8-family binding partners.
evidence: Established knowledge about Rab8 and Rab10 localization
